summary: Describes additional attributes for carrying authentication, authorization and accounting information between a Network Access Server and a shared server using RADIUS, building on RFC 2865 and RFC 2866. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo adds new items to the shared rules that a dial-in server and a central authentication server use to talk. The additions let the central server ask for regular usage reports, handle Apple Remote Access logins, and carry a flexible login method called EAP. It is an Informational memo, and later RFCs have updated it.

questions: what is the radius eap-message attribute
subtitle: New RADIUS attributes for interim accounting, Apple Remote Access, and carrying EAP through a RADIUS server.

tldr.problem: RADIUS as defined in RFC 2865 and RFC 2866 had no standard way to receive interim accounting updates, to authenticate Apple Remote Access users, or to pass EAP authentication between a dial-in server and a RADIUS server.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines new attributes (types 52 to 88) including Acct-Interim-Interval, the ARAP set, EAP-Message and Message-Authenticator. EAP packets travel inside EAP-Message attributes, and an HMAC-MD5 Message-Authenticator protects them.
tldr.outcome: The attributes had little field experience and were called experimental. The memo is Informational and has since been updated by RFC 3579 and RFC 5080.

facts.label: Acct-Interim-Interval
facts.value: Type 85; MUST NOT be below 60 seconds

today: RFC 2869 is an Informational memo and has been updated by RFC 3579 and RFC 5080. The metadata does not list an RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Extend RADIUS
sections.content:
RFC 2865 describes the RADIUS protocol and RFC 2866 describes accounting with it. This memo suggests several additional attributes for useful functions. The RFC says these attributes do not have extensive field experience yet and should be considered experimental.

Attributes are variable-length Type-Length-Value tuples, so new ones can be added without disturbing existing implementations. Operation, packet format and packet types are identical to those in RFC 2865 and RFC 2866.

One rule runs throughout: a NAS that does not implement a service MUST NOT implement the RADIUS attributes for that service, and it MUST treat an access-request for an unavailable service as an access-reject.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS lets one login server check names and passwords with a shared central server. The original rules were missing a few useful messages, so this memo adds them as optional extras that old software can ignore.

sections.title: Interim Accounting Updates
sections.content:
When a login succeeds, the RADIUS server sends an Access-Accept. To receive interim accounting messages for a user, the server includes the Acct-Interim-Interval attribute in that Access-Accept, giving the interval in seconds between updates. A value configured locally on the NAS MUST override the value in an Access-Accept.

This does not break backward interoperability: a server that does not support the extension simply does not add the attribute, and a NAS that does not support it ignores the attribute.

All information in an interim message is cumulative, so the packet count is the total since the session began. An interim record (Acct-Status-Type = Interim-Update (3)) should carry the attributes of an Accounting Stop message except Acct-Term-Cause. Because each message is cumulative, a NAS MUST keep only a single generation of an interim message per session in its retransmission queue, and a NAS MAY add a random delay so that updates from many sessions are not sent at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The central server can ask to be told how much each session has used, at a fixed interval. Each report gives the running total for the whole session, not just the amount since the last report.

sections.title: Apple Remote Access (ARAP) Support
sections.content:
The Apple Remote Access Protocol (ARAP) carries AppleTalk traffic over point-to-point links. Before this memo, ARAP connections on multi-protocol NAS devices were often not authenticated with RADIUS, or each vendor made its own solution. The memo adds a small set of ARAP attributes and assumes the RADIUS server can do DES encryption, keeping with the RADIUS goal of a smart server and a simple NAS.

ARAP authenticates in two phases. The first is a two-way DES random-number exchange using the user's password as the key, in which the NAS and the client each challenge the other. The second phase is optional and uses Apple's Add-In Security Modules, which the memo reduces to simple challenge and response cycles.

In the Access-Request the NAS sends the user name (up to 31 characters), a Framed-Protocol of 3 (ARAP), and ARAP-Password. That 16-octet value carries the dial-in user's challenge to the NAS (high-order 8 octets) and the user's response to the NAS challenge (low-order 8 octets). On success the server returns Access-Accept with ARAP-Challenge-Response and ARAP-Features; on failure it returns Access-Reject, optionally with Password-Retry.

The memo does not address user-initiated password changes or out-of-band messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Apple's dial-in software proves a user knows the password by scrambling random numbers with it, and the server does the same in return. The new items carry those scrambled numbers between the dial-in server and the central server.

sections.title: Carrying EAP Through RADIUS
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a PPP extension that supports many authentication methods. Two new attributes make it work over RADIUS: EAP-Message wraps EAP packets, and Message-Authenticator protects them. The NAS never needs to understand the EAP packets it forwards.

After EAP is negotiated in LCP, the NAS normally sends an EAP-Request/Identity to the peer, then forwards the reply in an Access-Request. To let EAP-unaware proxies forward the request, the NAS MUST copy the identity into the User-Name attribute. If no identity request is sent, the NAS can send an EAP-Message of length 2 with no data to signal EAP-Start, though this is not compatible with RFC 2865 and is hard to use with proxies.

A server that supports EAP MUST answer with an Access-Challenge carrying an EAP-Message; one that does not MUST answer Access-Reject. The conversation continues until an Access-Accept (with EAP-Success) or Access-Reject arrives. An Access-Reject MUST make the NAS send an LCP Terminate Request.

The NAS handles retransmission to the peer, while the RADIUS client handles retransmission to the server. The server can supply Session-Timeout and Password-Retry in an Access-Challenge, for example to give a token-card user more time, and the NAS can pass Framed-MTU so the server can size EAP packets. The memo also recommends RADIUS-encapsulated EAP between a RADIUS server and a backend security server.
sections.plainLanguage: The dial-in server passes sealed login messages between the visitor and the central server without reading them. Each message carries a stamp that shows it was not altered on the way.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
The memo defines these attribute types: Acct-Input-Gigawords (52), Acct-Output-Gigawords (53), Event-Timestamp (55), ARAP-Password (70), ARAP-Features (71), ARAP-Zone-Access (72), ARAP-Security (73), ARAP-Security-Data (74), Password-Retry (75), Prompt (76), Connect-Info (77), Configuration-Token (78), EAP-Message (79), Message-Authenticator (80), ARAP-Challenge-Response (84), Acct-Interim-Interval (85), NAS-Port-Id (87) and Framed-Pool (88).

The Gigawords attributes count how many times the 32-bit octet counters have wrapped around 2^32. Acct-Interim-Interval MUST NOT be smaller than 60 seconds and SHOULD NOT be smaller than 600. Message-Authenticator is 18 octets long and is an HMAC-MD5 over the whole packet using the shared secret as the key, computed with the attribute value treated as sixteen zero octets. Multiple EAP-Message attributes are concatenated so that EAP packets longer than 253 octets can be carried.

An Access-Request carrying a User-Password, CHAP-Password, ARAP-Password or EAP-Message MUST NOT contain more than one of those four types. Any packet that contains an EAP-Message MUST also contain a Message-Authenticator.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists each new item on the shared form, with its number so both sides know which one is meant. The list covers usage counters, Apple Remote Access details, and the items that carry EAP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Apart from Message-Authenticator and EAP-Message, the attributes add no security considerations beyond RFC 2865. The Message-Authenticator is needed because requests carrying a CHAP-Password or EAP-Message have no User-Password to establish the identity of the NAS. It is intended to stop a rogue NAS from making online dictionary attacks, but it gives no protection against offline attacks on captured CHAP exchanges. The RFC says IP Security will eventually make it unnecessary, so it is an interim measure.

For EAP, the memo discusses several risks. If the EAP server and the PPP authenticator are separate machines, mutual authentication is between the peer and the EAP server, so the peer cannot validate the NAS, and the session key needs a transport mechanism outside the memo's scope. Because RADIUS has no encryption and its integrity protection is weaker than some EAP methods, all EAP/RADIUS packets MUST use Message-Authenticator. Shared secrets give no end-to-end security across proxies, separate user databases are a weakness, and a negotiation attack can push a user to a weaker method. The defence is per-connection policy at the peer and per-user policy at the server, and a peer that expects EAP MUST NOT negotiate CHAP or PAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a stamp on each login message, a fake dial-in server could guess passwords or quietly swap in a weaker login method. The memo requires the stamp on EAP messages and tells clients to refuse any method weaker than the one they expected.
